title: Red Balloon

image.credit: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: An abstract painting by Paul Klee titled Red Balloon, made with chalk and oil on a panel. The title suggests a red balloon among simple, non-realistic forms.

source.museum: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An abstract work by Paul Klee made in 1922 with chalk and oil on a panel, now at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York. The source page tags it Abstract Art. Klee was teaching at the Bauhaus art school in Germany at this time.

descriptions.k: This painting is called Red Balloon. Look for the red balloon. Where do you think it is? Now find the other shapes and colors. What do they remind you of?
descriptions.g12: Paul Klee made Red Balloon in 1922. It is an abstract painting, so the shapes do not have to look like real things. Look for the balloon the title talks about. What other shapes do you see? What do they remind you of?
descriptions.g35: Paul Klee made Red Balloon in 1922 using chalk and oil paint on a panel. It is called abstract art, which means it uses shapes and colors in a free way instead of copying real life. Look for the balloon from the title. What shapes and colors does Klee use, and what do they make you imagine?
descriptions.g68: Klee's Red Balloon (1922) is an abstract work in chalk and oil on panel, made while he taught at the Bauhaus in Germany. The title offers a starting point, but abstract art leaves much for the viewer to decide. How do the shapes, colors and the title work together? Use what you can see to explain what you think the picture is showing, and say where another reading could fit.
descriptions.g910: Red Balloon (1922) was made in chalk and oil on panel by Paul Klee, who taught at the Bauhaus. The mixed medium combines a drawing material with paint, and the title gives an everyday object to an abstract composition. Consider how title and image negotiate between recognizable subject and invention. Where does the picture feel representational, and where does it resist being read literally?
descriptions.g1112: Klee's Red Balloon (1922), in chalk and oil on panel, comes from his Bauhaus years, when he combined teaching on color and form with inventive, often playful picture-making. The title seems to name an ordinary object while the picture operates in an abstract mode. How does the work hold recognition and abstraction in tension, and what does the combination of drawn and painted marks add? Support your reading with specific visual evidence and acknowledge alternatives.

k.daily: Look for the red balloon. Where do you see something red?
k.emotion: How does this painting make you feel? Happy, calm or silly?
k.observation: Point to a shape you can name. What is it?
k.analysis: Which part of the painting do you look at first?
k.line: Trace one line with your finger. Where does it go?
k.shape: Find a round shape. What do you think it could be?
k.color: Which colors can you name in this painting?
k.texture: This painting has chalk marks and paint. Which parts look chalky, and which look smooth?
k.space: Which shape is highest up? Which shape is lowest down?
k.light: Point to the brightest spot. What is it?
k.meaning: A balloon floats in the air. What would it be like to float away like a balloon?
k.culture: Klee taught art at a school in Germany. What would you like to learn at an art school?
k.technique: Klee used chalk and paint together. What would you make if you used both?
k.personal: If you could hold the balloon, where would you take it?
k.critical: What would you add to the painting to make it even more fun?

g12.daily: Why do you think Klee named this painting Red Balloon?
g12.emotion: What feeling does the painting give you, and which colors help make it?
g12.observation: Find three different shapes in the painting. Describe each one.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye go to the red part first?
g12.line: How do the lines in the painting go: straight, curvy or zigzag? Show one with your finger.
g12.shape: Which shapes look like they came from real things, and which look made up?
g12.color: How does the red look different from the colors around it?
g12.texture: Chalk makes dry, rough marks. Where do you think the chalk might be, and how does it look different from paint?
g12.space: Do the shapes look near or far? What makes you say that?
g12.light: Which parts look light and which parts look dark?
g12.meaning: What story could you tell about this painting? Begin with the red balloon.
g12.culture: Abstract art does not have to look real. Why might an artist choose to make art that way?
g12.technique: How can an artist use a chalk drawing and a painting together in one picture?
g12.personal: What would you name the painting if you had to choose a different title?
g12.critical: How would the painting change if the balloon were blue?

g35.daily: What do you think Klee wants you to notice first, and which parts of the painting lead you there?
g35.emotion: What mood do the colors and shapes create, and what details help you decide?
g35.observation: Describe the red balloon in the painting, or what you think it is, and the shapes around it.
g35.analysis: How does Klee balance the balloon with the other shapes in the picture?
g35.line: What kinds of lines do you see, and how do they move your eye around?
g35.shape: Which shapes could stand for real objects, and which look like pure shapes?
g35.color: How does the red balloon stand out from, or fit with, the other colors?
g35.texture: How do the chalk and oil paint make different marks, and where do you see the difference?
g35.space: How does Klee show space, near and far, in a picture that is not realistic?
g35.light: How do the lighter and darker areas change how the shapes feel?
g35.meaning: Abstract art lets viewers imagine their own meaning. What does the balloon stand for in your imagination?
g35.culture: Klee taught at a famous art school called the Bauhaus. What might students there have learned from looking at his work?
g35.technique: Why might an artist combine a drawing material like chalk with paint?
g35.personal: What questions would you ask Klee about this painting?
g35.critical: How is an abstract painting different from a painting that copies what a balloon really looks like?

g68.daily: How does the title Red Balloon guide the way you read the abstract forms?
g68.emotion: How do color and shape together create the emotional tone of the painting?
g68.observation: Where do you see recognizable forms and where do you see pure invention? Describe the contrast.
g68.analysis: How does Klee arrange the forms so that the balloon becomes, or does not become, the focal point?
g68.line: How do lines and edges differ in character, and what effect does that have on the picture's rhythm?
g68.shape: How do geometric and organic shapes interact in the composition?
g68.color: How does the use of red against the surrounding colors create emphasis or tension?
g68.texture: How does the combination of chalk and oil paint create contrasts of surface, and where do you notice them?
g68.space: How does Klee suggest depth or flatness in a work that is not trying to be realistic?
g68.light: How do areas of light and dark help organize the picture without a clear light source?
g68.meaning: What different meanings could the balloon suggest, and what visual evidence supports each?
g68.culture: The Bauhaus encouraged artists to study color and form closely. How might this influence show in the work?
g68.technique: What is the advantage of mixing a drawing medium with painting in a single work?
g68.personal: If you made an abstract picture from a simple object, what would you choose and how would you change it?
g68.critical: Why might abstract art need an explanation, or not need one, to be enjoyed? Use this painting to argue your view.

g910.daily: How does the title shape the way you search for meaning in an abstract arrangement of forms?
g910.emotion: What emotional register do the palette and the character of the marks establish?
g910.observation: Examine the marks made with chalk versus those made with paint. What can you infer about Klee's working process?
g910.analysis: How does the arrangement of forms create visual hierarchy, and how does the red element function within it?
g910.line: How does the quality of line, whether tentative, confident or playful, affect the character of the whole?
g910.shape: How do geometric and irregular shapes create a tension between order and spontaneity?
g910.color: How does the use of a strong red against its surroundings generate emphasis, and what alternative palette might change the mood?
g910.texture: What does the combination of a dry drawing medium and oil paint suggest about the layering of the image?
g910.space: How does Klee handle spatial ambiguity, and does the picture ask you to read depth or flatness?
g910.light: How does tonal variation, in the absence of a single light source, build structure in the picture?
g910.meaning: How does the painting use an everyday object as a point of entry into abstraction?
g910.culture: How does the Bauhaus context, with its focus on teaching form and color, help in reading a work like this?
g910.technique: How does the mixed medium extend what a painting can be in 1922, and what does it say about Klee's experimentation?
g910.personal: What does your response to this picture reveal about how you interpret images that do not look realistic?
g910.critical: To what extent does recognition of the balloon matter to the painting's success, and how would you argue either way?

g1112.daily: How does Red Balloon sustain a dialogue between naming and not naming, and what does that reveal about how abstraction relies on language?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the interplay of saturated color and delicate marks create an emotional register that resists easy description?
g1112.observation: What can the physical evidence of chalk and oil on panel suggest about the sequence of decisions Klee made?
g1112.analysis: How does the composition distribute weight and attention, and where does it deliberately withhold a clear focal point, if it does?
g1112.line: How might the character of line in the painting show Klee's well-known interest in drawing as a form of thought?
g1112.shape: How do geometric and organic forms collaborate or conflict, and what might that suggest about the balance between system and intuition?
g1112.color: How does the chromatic structure function as an argument about the power of a single hue, and what would you test to evaluate that claim?
g1112.texture: How does the mixture of media complicate the boundary between drawing and painting?
g1112.space: How does the picture's spatial logic compare with the conventions of illusionistic depth, and what is gained by departing from them?
g1112.light: How does the distribution of tone organize the picture in the absence of naturalistic illumination?
g1112.meaning: Is it more productive to treat the balloon as symbol, as motif or as pure form? Defend your approach using the evidence available.
g1112.culture: How does Klee's position within the Bauhaus, as a teacher of form theory, complicate or enrich the reading of what might look like a spontaneous image?
g1112.technique: What does the combination of chalk and oil reveal about early twentieth-century debates over the purity of media?
g1112.personal: How does your own tolerance for ambiguity influence the interpretation you reach, and what does that say about abstract art?
g1112.critical: Make the strongest case that a small, seemingly playful abstract work can be as intellectually serious as a large academic painting, and say how you would test it.

teacherNote.context: An abstract work by Paul Klee, made in 1922 with chalk and oil on panel and held by the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York. Klee taught at the Bauhaus school in Germany in these years.
directions: Have students look silently for one minute, then name every shape and color they see before discussing the title.
Ask younger students to make their own balloon picture using chalk and paint, using shapes that do not have to look real.
Ask older students to debate how much a title should guide the way we read an abstract work.
